newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. speciality coffee market seen "consolidating".
newsitem.headline: U.S. speciality coffee market seen "consolidating".

text.p: The surge in world coffee prices earlier this year is likely to trigger a flurry of mergers and acquisitions in the U.S. speciality coffee market, a leading industry official said.

"The price rise of 1997 has really caused lots of people, if they weren't thinking about it already, to think about merging with some of their counterparts," said Ted Lingle, executive director of the Specialty Coffee Association of America (SCAA).
Lingle, who spoke in an interview with Reuters late on Monday, was in Medellin for an event on Tuesday marking the 70th anniversary of Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation.

In the interview, Lingle said he was reluctant to predict that the speciality market had peaked after 30 years of growth. But he conceded that 1995 was "probably the highwater mark" for speciality coffee in the United States and said "tremendous growth" had left the industry vulnerable to a "shake-out."
"What we think is going to happen with specialty coffee is that it will go through a classic sort of growth curve, where it took off for a while and then there's a period of consolidation," he said.
"It was just inevitable," he added. "You can't have so many new people coming into the industry so ill-prepared for what it involves and not have some shake-out."
Lingle was not specific about what sort of mergers he saw on the horizon as part of the "realignment" which he said was already under way in the speciality market in the U.S.

But he noted that Starbucks Corp's "very successful stock offering" in 1991 was another industry highwater mark. He also said the market was likely to see a series of strategic partnerships taking place between retailers and wholesalers as part of a bid to jump-start "another period of rapid growth."
At present, Lingle said speciality coffees account for up to three million 60-kg bags of the 18 million bags of coffee consumed yearly in the United States.

According to Lingle, one of the leading curbs on expansion in the U.S. speciality market was tight supply -- and the fact that there simply was not enough coffee like Colombia's "benchmark origin" to grow the market.
"One of the problems the industry faces is that demand for these coffees has grown faster than the growth of supply," he said. "That's why we're looking at a $2 dollar New York market."
"There's no short-term fix," he added. "It still takes some three to five years for the decision to invest (in bigger harvests) to actively result in sellable products."
